Documented limitations of the incumbent approach are calibration-transfer accuracy (the CVR-to-B-dot transfer function must be re-established per geometry), near-load survivability against blast, debris, and x-ray-induced EMP (Webb 2023), and the well-known bandwidth/electric-field-pickup weaknesses of Rogowski coils specifically noted in gas-puff/DPF contexts. Radiation here is a brief, intense burst (hard x-ray flash, ns-timescale) rather than the cumulative fluence regime this mission's radiation lane is built around, so it stresses shot-to-shot electronics survivability and shielding rather than long-term semiconductor degradation ΓÇö a materially different failure mode than what the Hall-material radiation literature (folder 06 / lane 10B) addresses. On fit: the evidence argues against a Hall+coil hybrid here. Hall devices are independently documented as bandwidth-limited (practically DC-to-hundreds-of-kHz, at best ~1 MHz with exotic materials) and acutely EMI-susceptible, especially to tangential RF E-fields (Aiello 2019) ΓÇö and while that source is drawn from power-electronics testing rather than a z-pinch facility itself (an extrapolation I am flagging explicitly, not asserting as z-pinch-validated), the qualitative mechanism (E-field coupling into a low-level Hall bias) would only be worse in a near-MITL/near-convolute environment with kV/m-scale transient fields. Critically, the domain's own literature already shows the community solved its dual-need-for-redundancy problem by fusing two inductive sensors (B-dot + Rogowski) rather than reaching for a DC-capable Hall channel (Moffett 2022) ΓÇö direct prior art suggesting no unmet need for Hall-derived absolute-field information at these timescales, since the "DC" information a Hall sensor would add is irrelevant when the entire event lives inside one sub-microsecond pulse with no persistent DC baseline to track. Calibration and validation access is comparatively good relative to other lanes: CVR-referenced radial-transmission-line calibration stands exist at Sandia (Wagoner 2008), and standalone bench cross-calibration protocols are published and reproducible (Moffett 2022) ΓÇö but that access serves pure-inductive diagnostics, not a Hall+coil hybrid, and provides no natural entry point for validating a Hall channel's gain/offset in a regime where the "DC/quasi-static segment" required by this mission's decision framework for Hall-vs-coil observability essentially does not exist within a single shot.

## Prose synthesis

The z-pinch/pulsed-power lane is defined by extremes that are essentially opposite to the HSX regime: currents from ~0.5 MA (university-scale gas-puff and MAGPIE drivers, Conti 2024; Halliday 2022) up to 20-30 MA (Sandia Z, Wagoner 2008; Webb 2023), with current/field rise times of 100-240 ns and, in the AutoMag sub-case, dI/dt as high as 200 kA/ns (Shipley 2018, 2019) ΓÇö three to six orders of magnitude faster than any signal this mission's Hall+coil architecture is designed around. The incumbent diagnostics are exclusively inductive: B-dot probes and Rogowski coils, cross-calibrated against a current-viewing resistor (CVR) reference on a dedicated calibrated test stand (Wagoner 2008), and increasingly fused with each other in "sensor fusion" protocols that never invoke a Hall channel (Moffett 2022, achieving ┬▒13-15% error fusing B-dot + Rogowski). Documented limitations of the incumbent approach are calibration-transfer accuracy (the CVR-to-B-dot transfer function must be re-established per geometry), near-load survivability against blast, debris, and x-ray-induced EMP (Webb 2023), and the well-known bandwidth/electric-field-pickup weaknesses of Rogowski coils specifically noted in gas-puff/DPF contexts. Radiation here is a brief, intense burst (hard x-ray flash, ns-timescale) rather than the cumulative fluence regime this mission's radiation lane is built around, so it stresses shot-to-shot electronics survivability and shielding rather than long-term semiconductor degradation ΓÇö a materially different failure mode than what the Hall-material radiation literature (folder 06 / lane 10B) addresses. On fit: the evidence argues against a Hall+coil hybrid here. Hall devices are independently documented as bandwidth-limited (practically DC-to-hundreds-of-kHz, at best ~1 MHz with exotic materials) and acutely EMI-susceptible, especially to tangential RF E-fields (Aiello 2019) ΓÇö and while that source is drawn from power-electronics testing rather than a z-pinch facility itself (an extrapolation I am flagging explicitly, not asserting as z-pinch-validated), the qualitative mechanism (E-field coupling into a low-level Hall bias) would only be worse in a near-MITL/near-convolute environment with kV/m-scale transient fields. Critically, the domain's own literature already shows the community solved its dual-need-for-redundancy problem by fusing two inductive sensors (B-dot + Rogowski) rather than reaching for a DC-capable Hall channel (Moffett 2022) ΓÇö direct prior art suggesting no unmet need for Hall-derived absolute-field information at these timescales, since the "DC" information a Hall sensor would add is irrelevant when the entire event lives inside one sub-microsecond pulse with no persistent DC baseline to track. Calibration and validation access is comparatively good relative to other lanes: CVR-referenced radial-transmission-line calibration stands exist at Sandia (Wagoner 2008), and standalone bench cross-calibration protocols are published and reproducible (Moffett 2022) ΓÇö but that access serves pure-inductive diagnostics, not a Hall+coil hybrid, and provides no natural entry point for validating a Hall channel's gain/offset in a regime where the "DC/quasi-static segment" required by this mission's decision framework for Hall-vs-coil observability essentially does not exist within a single shot.

## Prose synthesis

This is a genuinely thin, low-publication-volume field for magnetic-diagnostic-specific literature compared to tokamak/stellarator work: most PLX/HyperV/ZaP/MagLIF papers report plasma dynamics or fusion performance and treat the B-dot/Hall probe array as a supporting-methods paragraph rather than the subject of the paper, so directly-on-topic sensor papers are scarce. The incumbent diagnostic across this whole family is the multi-axis B-dot (Mirnov-style) coil array ΓÇö used at PLX to time liner-jet impact and infer axis offset/circularity (Hsu 2015, JPP), embedded at the electrode/boundary in Z-pinches to infer pinch radius via inductance cross-checked against circuit models (Rousskikh 2018), and used for boundary-region field/current inference in MagLIF (Hansen 2015). Field magnitudes and bandwidths vary enormously by platform: from sub-Tesla bias fields with microsecond-scale pinch dynamics (Rousskikh; Shumlak's review) to the tens-of-Tesla, mega-ampere, tens-of-nanosecond regime at the MagLIF load (Hansen; Hess). Two clear, documented limitations of the coil-only incumbent emerge: (1) where fields, EMI, and mechanical/thermal stress are most extreme ΓÇö the MagLIF power-feed/load region ΓÇö practitioners abandon magnetic sensing altogether in favor of optical (PDV) current inference (Hess 2018), and (2) where the field must be measured inside the hot, dense plasma column itself rather than at a boundary, magnetic probes are physically unusable and spectroscopic Zeeman splitting is substituted instead (Golingo 2010, ZaP). Neither gap is naturally closed by a Hall+coil hybrid: a Hall element adds no survivability in the load-adjacent EMI/thermal environment where the coil itself is already marginal, and neither Hall nor coil can be inserted into the pinch core where Zeeman spectroscopy is used precisely because in-situ probes cannot survive there. Where hybrid Hall+coil sensing could plausibly add value is at boundary/wall locations in lower-field, lower-repetition, single-shot devices (PLX-class jets, ZaP-HD boundary array) if a stable pre-shot calibration reference (bench Helmholtz/traceable field plus circuit-model cross-check, as already practiced informally in Rousskikh 2018) is available ΓÇö but none of the sources found here demonstrate or propose an actual Hall+coil fusion in this domain; this is an evidence gap, not a documented result. Calibration access in this domain is dominated by pre-shot bench calibration and post-hoc circuit-model consistency checks (voltage/current/inductance), not embedded in-situ reference coils or dosimetry; the single-shot, destructive-liner nature of most of these experiments (with Zap Energy's repetitive Century platform as the clear counter-example) makes a stable DC reference difficult to maintain shot-to-shot, which is the same structural-identifiability problem the mission's decision framework flags for Hall gain/offset drift. Radiation environment differs sharply by sub-field and must not be merged: MagLIF documents significant DD/DT neutron yield (~10^12 neutrons, Hansen 2015) while PLX/HyperV plasma-jet and ZaP/ZaP-HD/Century experiments are non-fusion or low-yield and radiation is not a first-order constraint in the sources found. Overall I found 8 verified, new, directly relevant peer-reviewed sources against a target of 5-9, but 7 of the 8 required abstract/metadata-level verification (no full-text access), and the 8th (Zap Energy Century) is metadata-verified only with technical claims explicitly withheld ΓÇö this is an honest reflection of a niche field where much of the technical detail sits behind paywalls or in press releases rather than open full text.

## Prose synthesis

This is a genuinely thin, low-publication-volume field for magnetic-diagnostic-specific literature compared to tokamak/stellarator work: most PLX/HyperV/ZaP/MagLIF papers report plasma dynamics or fusion performance and treat the B-dot/Hall probe array as a supporting-methods paragraph rather than the subject of the paper, so directly-on-topic sensor papers are scarce. The incumbent diagnostic across this whole family is the multi-axis B-dot (Mirnov-style) coil array ΓÇö used at PLX to time liner-jet impact and infer axis offset/circularity (Hsu 2015, JPP), embedded at the electrode/boundary in Z-pinches to infer pinch radius via inductance cross-checked against circuit models (Rousskikh 2018), and used for boundary-region field/current inference in MagLIF (Hansen 2015). Field magnitudes and bandwidths vary enormously by platform: from sub-Tesla bias fields with microsecond-scale pinch dynamics (Rousskikh; Shumlak's review) to the tens-of-Tesla, mega-ampere, tens-of-nanosecond regime at the MagLIF load (Hansen; Hess). Two clear, documented limitations of the coil-only incumbent emerge: (1) where fields, EMI, and mechanical/thermal stress are most extreme ΓÇö the MagLIF power-feed/load region ΓÇö practitioners abandon magnetic sensing altogether in favor of optical (PDV) current inference (Hess 2018), and (2) where the field must be measured inside the hot, dense plasma column itself rather than at a boundary, magnetic probes are physically unusable and spectroscopic Zeeman splitting is substituted instead (Golingo 2010, ZaP). Neither gap is naturally closed by a Hall+coil hybrid: a Hall element adds no survivability in the load-adjacent EMI/thermal environment where the coil itself is already marginal, and neither Hall nor coil can be inserted into the pinch core where Zeeman spectroscopy is used precisely because in-situ probes cannot survive there. Where hybrid Hall+coil sensing could plausibly add value is at boundary/wall locations in lower-field, lower-repetition, single-shot devices (PLX-class jets, ZaP-HD boundary array) if a stable pre-shot calibration reference (bench Helmholtz/traceable field plus circuit-model cross-check, as already practiced informally in Rousskikh 2018) is available ΓÇö but none of the sources found here demonstrate or propose an actual Hall+coil fusion in this domain; this is an evidence gap, not a documented result. Calibration access in this domain is dominated by pre-shot bench calibration and post-hoc circuit-model consistency checks (voltage/current/inductance), not embedded in-situ reference coils or dosimetry; the single-shot, destructive-liner nature of most of these experiments (with Zap Energy's repetitive Century platform as the clear counter-example) makes a stable DC reference difficult to maintain shot-to-shot, which is the same structural-identifiability problem the mission's decision framework flags for Hall gain/offset drift. Radiation environment differs sharply by sub-field and must not be merged: MagLIF documents significant DD/DT neutron yield (~10^12 neutrons, Hansen 2015) while PLX/HyperV plasma-jet and ZaP/ZaP-HD/Century experiments are non-fusion or low-yield and radiation is not a first-order constraint in the sources found. ## Prose synthesis

This is a genuinely thin, low-publication-volume field for magnetic-diagnostic-specific literature compared to tokamak/stellarator work: most PLX/HyperV/ZaP/MagLIF papers report plasma dynamics or fusion performance and treat the B-dot/Hall probe array as a supporting-methods paragraph rather than the subject of the paper, so directly-on-topic sensor papers are scarce. The incumbent diagnostic across this whole family is the multi-axis B-dot (Mirnov-style) coil array ΓÇö used at PLX to time liner-jet impact and infer axis offset/circularity (Hsu 2015, JPP), embedded at the electrode/boundary in Z-pinches to infer pinch radius via inductance cross-checked against circuit models (Rousskikh 2018), and used for boundary-region field/current inference in MagLIF (Hansen 2015). Field magnitudes and bandwidths vary enormously by platform: from sub-Tesla bias fields with microsecond-scale pinch dynamics (Rousskikh; Shumlak's review) to the tens-of-Tesla, mega-ampere, tens-of-nanosecond regime at the MagLIF load (Hansen; Hess). Two clear, documented limitations of the coil-only incumbent emerge: (1) where fields, EMI, and mechanical/thermal stress are most extreme ΓÇö the MagLIF power-feed/load region ΓÇö practitioners abandon magnetic sensing altogether in favor of optical (PDV) current inference (Hess 2018), and (2) where the field must be measured inside the hot, dense plasma column itself rather than at a boundary, magnetic probes are physically unusable and spectroscopic Zeeman splitting is substituted instead (Golingo 2010, ZaP). Neither gap is naturally closed by a Hall+coil hybrid: a Hall element adds no survivability in the load-adjacent EMI/thermal environment where the coil itself is already marginal, and neither Hall nor coil can be inserted into the pinch core where Zeeman spectroscopy is used precisely because in-situ probes cannot survive there. Where hybrid Hall+coil sensing could plausibly add value is at boundary/wall locations in lower-field, lower-repetition, single-shot devices (PLX-class jets, ZaP-HD boundary array) if a stable pre-shot calibration reference (bench Helmholtz/traceable field plus circuit-model cross-check, as already practiced informally in Rousskikh 2018) is available ΓÇö but none of the sources found here demonstrate or propose an actual Hall+coil fusion in this domain; this is an evidence gap, not a documented result. Calibration access in this domain is dominated by pre-shot bench calibration and post-hoc circuit-model consistency checks (voltage/current/inductance), not embedded in-situ reference coils or dosimetry; the single-shot, destructive-liner nature of most of these experiments (with Zap Energy's repetitive Century platform as the clear counter-example) makes a stable DC reference difficult to maintain shot-to-shot, which is the same structural-identifiability problem the mission's decision framework flags for Hall gain/offset drift. Radiation environment differs sharply by sub-field and must not be merged: MagLIF documents significant DD/DT neutron yield (~10^12 neutrons, Hansen 2015) while PLX/HyperV plasma-jet and ZaP/ZaP-HD/Century experiments are non-fusion or low-yield and radiation is not a first-order constraint in the sources found. Overall I found 8 verified, new, directly relevant peer-reviewed sources against a target of 5-9, but 7 of the 8 required abstract/metadata-level verification (no full-text access), and the 8th (Zap Energy Century) is metadata-verified only with technical claims explicitly withheld ΓÇö this is an honest reflection of a niche field where much of the technical detail sits behind paywalls or in press releases rather than open full text.

## Synthesis

Combined Hall-probe + rotating-coil (+NMR) magnetic field mapping is not a novel hybrid concept in the accelerator-magnet world ΓÇö it is decades-old, routine, production-scale incumbent practice. LHC dipoles (all 1232 of them) were characterized with long twin rotating-coil shafts, and CERN/FNAL groups (Arpaia, Buzio, Russenschuck, Golluccio, Rogacki, Fiscarelli and collaborators) have continued refining rotating-coil transducers (flexible PCB coils, miniaturized/small-bore scanners, HL-LHC inner-triplet scanners) through 2019-2022, consistently pairing them with NMR or reference-magnet calibration and, per search-surfaced evidence, with Hall probes for local/end-field mapping where the rotating coil's integral-only measurement is insufficient. NMR remains the field's gold-standard absolute reference (Prigl et al. 1996 established sub-10^-7 precision NMR magnetometry for accelerator/storage-ring use; Rodriguez et al. 2020 treats NMR calibration-reference physics generally), and access to an NMR reference is standard rather than exotic in this community, unlike in fusion in-vessel environments. The documented incumbent limitation is the mirror image of the mission's own confounding problem: Hall probes give absolute, spatially-resolved field values but need frequent recalibration against NMR/reference magnets and are the fallback for non-uniform end/fringe regions, while rotating coils give very high precision (ppm-level, 100 ppm cited for HL-LHC inner triplets) integral/harmonic content but require precise mechanical rotation references, in-situ area/radius calibration (Arpaia et al. 2012), and cannot resolve local point fields ΓÇö exactly the DC-absolute-vs-AC-integral complementarity the mission is evaluating, already solved operationally at CERN/FNAL/HIAF scale for multi-Tesla, quasi-static/ramped (not fast-pulsed) fields with long, controlled measurement cycles in narrow magnet bores. Radiation in this literature set is present mainly as background context (HL-LHC arc radiation environment) rather than as a mapping-bench qualification driver, since mapping benches typically operate outside the beamline during dedicated magnet-test campaigns rather than in-situ during beam operation ΓÇö this is a material contrast with the mission's in-vessel/near-plasma use case and should be flagged as a scope difference, not assumed away. Net effect for the mission's novelty question: this is a real prior-art concern for any claim that "Hall+coil fusion" itself is new; the mission's potential differentiator, if any, would need to rest on the radiation/in-situ/embedded-calibration angle rather than on the sensor-fusion architecture itself.

## Synthesis

Combined Hall-probe + rotating-coil (+NMR) magnetic field mapping is not a novel hybrid concept in the accelerator-magnet world ΓÇö it is decades-old, routine, production-scale incumbent practice. LHC dipoles (all 1232 of them) were characterized with long twin rotating-coil shafts, and CERN/FNAL groups (Arpaia, Buzio, Russenschuck, Golluccio, Rogacki, Fiscarelli and collaborators) have continued refining rotating-coil transducers (flexible PCB coils, miniaturized/small-bore scanners, HL-LHC inner-triplet scanners) through 2019-2022, consistently pairing them with NMR or reference-magnet calibration and, per search-surfaced evidence, with Hall probes for local/end-field mapping where the rotating coil's integral-only measurement is insufficient. NMR remains the field's gold-standard absolute reference (Prigl et al. 1996 established sub-10^-7 precision NMR magnetometry for accelerator/storage-ring use; Rodriguez et al. 2020 treats NMR calibration-reference physics generally), and access to an NMR reference is standard rather than exotic in this community, unlike in fusion in-vessel environments. The documented incumbent limitation is the mirror image of the mission's own confounding problem: Hall probes give absolute, spatially-resolved field values but need frequent recalibration against NMR/reference magnets and are the fallback for non-uniform end/fringe regions, while rotating coils give very high precision (ppm-level, 100 ppm cited for HL-LHC inner triplets) integral/harmonic content but require precise mechanical rotation references, in-situ area/radius calibration (Arpaia et al. 2012), and cannot resolve local point fields ΓÇö exactly the DC-absolute-vs-AC-integral complementarity the mission is evaluating, already solved operationally at CERN/FNAL/HIAF scale for multi-Tesla, quasi-static/ramped (not fast-pulsed) fields with long, controlled measurement cycles in narrow magnet bores. Radiation in this literature set is present mainly as background context (HL-LHC arc radiation environment) rather than as a mapping-bench qualification driver, since mapping benches typically operate outside the beamline during dedicated magnet-test campaigns rather than in-situ during beam operation ΓÇö this is a material contrast with the mission's in-vessel/near-plasma use case and should be flagged as a scope difference, not assumed away. Net effect for the mission's novelty question: this is a real prior-art concern for any claim that "Hall+coil fusion" itself is new; the mission's potential differentiator, if any, would need to rest on the radiation/in-situ/embedded-calibration angle rather than on the sensor-fusion architecture itself.

**Gate status for this domain contribution:** 8 new verified peer-reviewed sources delivered (within the 6-10 target), all confirmed absent from `dedup_baseline_dois.txt` (359-entry list) by exact-DOI grep. All access levels are `abstract_metadata` (Crossref/publisher metadata plus abstract-level content inspected via WebFetch/WebSearch; no full-text PDFs were opened), so none should be upgraded to `full_text` without a follow-up read. Two items need a flagged follow-up before being treated as hard fact in later stages: the Rogacki et al. numeric precision figures (100 ppm / 0.1 mrad / 0.1 mm) came from a search-engine abstract paraphrase, not a directly re-read abstract; and the Prigl et al. DOI (`10.1016/0168-9002(96)37493-7`) should get a direct `doi.org` resolution check since this session's direct fetch to that DOI was not completed (only Crossref bibliographic-search matches, consistent across two independent queries, were obtained).

## Synthesis

Combined Hall-probe + rotating-coil (+NMR) magnetic field mapping is not a novel hybrid concept in the accelerator-magnet world ΓÇö it is decades-old, routine, production-scale incumbent practice. LHC dipoles (all 1232 of them) were characterized with long twin rotating-coil shafts, and CERN/FNAL groups (Arpaia, Buzio, Russenschuck, Golluccio, Rogacki, Fiscarelli and collaborators) have continued refining rotating-coil transducers (flexible PCB coils, miniaturized/small-bore scanners, HL-LHC inner-triplet scanners) through 2019-2022, consistently pairing them with NMR or reference-magnet calibration and, per search-surfaced evidence, with Hall probes for local/end-field mapping where the rotating coil's integral-only measurement is insufficient. NMR remains the field's gold-standard absolute reference (Prigl et al. 1996 established sub-10^-7 precision NMR magnetometry for accelerator/storage-ring use; Rodriguez et al. 2020 treats NMR calibration-reference physics generally), and access to an NMR reference is standard rather than exotic in this community, unlike in fusion in-vessel environments. The documented incumbent limitation is the mirror image of the mission's own confounding problem: Hall probes give absolute, spatially-resolved field values but need frequent recalibration against NMR/reference magnets and are the fallback for non-uniform end/fringe regions, while rotating coils give very high precision (ppm-level, 100 ppm cited for HL-LHC inner triplets) integral/harmonic content but require precise mechanical rotation references, in-situ area/radius calibration (Arpaia et al. 2012), and cannot resolve local point fields ΓÇö exactly the DC-absolute-vs-AC-integral complementarity the mission is evaluating, already solved operationally at CERN/FNAL/HIAF scale for multi-Tesla, quasi-static/ramped (not fast-pulsed) fields with long, controlled measurement cycles in narrow magnet bores. Radiation in this literature set is present mainly as background context (HL-LHC arc radiation environment) rather than as a mapping-bench qualification driver, since mapping benches typically operate outside the beamline during dedicated magnet-test campaigns rather than in-situ during beam operation ΓÇö this is a material contrast with the mission's in-vessel/near-plasma use case and should be flagged as a scope difference, not assumed away. Net effect for the mission's novelty question: this is a real prior-art concern for any claim that "Hall+coil fusion" itself is new; the mission's potential differentiator, if any, would need to rest on the radiation/in-situ/embedded-calibration angle rather than on the sensor-fusion architecture itself.

**Gate status for this domain contribution:** 8 new verified peer-reviewed sources delivered (within the 6-10 target), all confirmed absent from `dedup_baseline_dois.txt` (359-entry list) by exact-DOI grep. All access levels are `abstract_metadata` (Crossref/publisher metadata plus abstract-level content inspected via WebFetch/WebSearch; no full-text PDFs were opened), so none should be upgraded to `full_text` without a follow-up read. Two items need a flagged follow-up before being treated as hard fact in later stages: the Rogacki et al. numeric precision figures (100 ppm / 0.1 mrad / 0.1 mm) came from a search-engine abstract paraphrase, not a directly re-read abstract; and the Prigl et al. DOI (`10.1016/0168-9002(96)37493-7`) should get a direct `doi.org` resolution check since this session's direct fetch to that DOI was not completed (only Crossref bibliographic-search matches, consistent across two independent queries, were obtained).

## Prose synthesis (domain: superconducting magnets / HTS field shaping / trapped-field rotors / superconducting motors-generators)

Field magnitudes in this lane are extreme relative to plasma-diagnostic work: bulk HTS trapped-field magnets now reach a documented record of 17.7 T (Patel et al. 2018, doi:10.1088/1361-6668/aad34c) with earlier 17.6 T (Durrell et al. 2014) and >17 T composite-stack (Huang et al. 2019/2020) results, all achieved by field-cooled or pulsed-field magnetization and then held as a static, persistent, essentially DC field for the operational lifetime of the magnet ΓÇö there is no continuous ramping once the magnet is charged. Superconducting-motor and generator field poles operate in the same DC-trapped regime at 35-77 K (Watasaki et al. 2021, doi:10.1088/1361-6668/abda5b; Climente-Alarcon et al. 2020, doi:10.1109/tasc.2020.2976603; Wang et al. 2023, doi:10.1088/1361-6668/acfcdf), with only the brief magnetization pulse itself (milliseconds, high dB/dt) constituting an AC/transient event. Cryostat access is the dominant spatial constraint: sensors are mounted at fixed points inside a cold bore or on a cryocooled rotor (4-77 K), commonly via linear or rotating Hall-sensor arrays (5-18 sensors) rather than a scanning bench probe, because in-situ access during operation is severely limited (Tsui et al. 2022, doi:10.1088/1361-6668/ac74e7). Temperature, not radiation, is the dominant environmental stressor, and cryogenic Hall behavior is quantitatively documented: InSb/GaAs epitaxial Hall sensors show sensitivity temperature coefficients that can be engineered down to ~0.001%/K in the 1.8-250 K range through doping (Oszwaldowski & Berus 2006, 2007), and other literature found during discovery (not yet independently ledger-verified here) reports sensitivity increasing by several percent from 320 K to 5 K before flattening below ~50 K ΓÇö i.e., cryogenic Hall sensors require their own low-temperature calibration curve, not a simple room-temperature transfer. The incumbent diagnostic for both trapped-field bulk magnets and superconducting-machine field poles is scanning or fixed-array Hall-probe mapping (Hengstberger et al. 2009; Perkins et al. 2001), with pick-up/search coils used only during the transient magnetization pulse itself (Eckert et al. 2001) ΓÇö never for the subsequent static state. This is the clearest domain-level confirmation of the mission's central concern: a coil channel is structurally blind to a persistent-mode trapped field because there is no dB/dt to sense once magnetization is complete, so a Hall+coil hybrid offers no incremental information in steady persistent-mode operation and only plausible value during the magnetization pulse (bandwidth/transient capture) or during in-machine AC ripple superimposed on the DC trapped field. The calibration-reference literature strongly favors NMR over any coil-based approach for the static state: the persistent-mode NMR magnet work (Yanagisawa et al. 2021, doi:10.1088/1361-6668/ac2120) shows a Hall sensor used only for coarse initial tracking, with the precision cross-check and long-term drift monitoring performed by an NMR Teslameter and a room-temperature solution-NMR probe ΓÇö exactly the material-diverse, independent reference the mission's decision framework calls for. Net assessment: this lane is a poor fit for the proposed Hall+coil hybrid's core value proposition (mutual drift calibration between two continuously co-observing channels), because the coil channel has no signal to contribute during the dominant (persistent/DC) operating mode; it is a plausible fit only as a transient/pulse-capture add-on during magnetization, where NMR (not the coil) remains the accepted absolute reference.

## Prose synthesis (domain: superconducting magnets / HTS field shaping / trapped-field rotors / superconducting motors-generators)

Field magnitudes in this lane are extreme relative to plasma-diagnostic work: bulk HTS trapped-field magnets now reach a documented record of 17.7 T (Patel et al. 2018, doi:10.1088/1361-6668/aad34c) with earlier 17.6 T (Durrell et al. 2014) and >17 T composite-stack (Huang et al. 2019/2020) results, all achieved by field-cooled or pulsed-field magnetization and then held as a static, persistent, essentially DC field for the operational lifetime of the magnet ΓÇö there is no continuous ramping once the magnet is charged. Superconducting-motor and generator field poles operate in the same DC-trapped regime at 35-77 K (Watasaki et al. 2021, doi:10.1088/1361-6668/abda5b; Climente-Alarcon et al. 2020, doi:10.1109/tasc.2020.2976603; Wang et al. 2023, doi:10.1088/1361-6668/acfcdf), with only the brief magnetization pulse itself (milliseconds, high dB/dt) constituting an AC/transient event. Cryostat access is the dominant spatial constraint: sensors are mounted at fixed points inside a cold bore or on a cryocooled rotor (4-77 K), commonly via linear or rotating Hall-sensor arrays (5-18 sensors) rather than a scanning bench probe, because in-situ access during operation is severely limited (Tsui et al. 2022, doi:10.1088/1361-6668/ac74e7). Temperature, not radiation, is the dominant environmental stressor, and cryogenic Hall behavior is quantitatively documented: InSb/GaAs epitaxial Hall sensors show sensitivity temperature coefficients that can be engineered down to ~0.001%/K in the 1.8-250 K range through doping (Oszwaldowski & Berus 2006, 2007), and other literature found during discovery (not yet independently ledger-verified here) reports sensitivity increasing by several percent from 320 K to 5 K before flattening below ~50 K ΓÇö i.e., cryogenic Hall sensors require their own low-temperature calibration curve, not a simple room-temperature transfer. The incumbent diagnostic for both trapped-field bulk magnets and superconducting-machine field poles is scanning or fixed-array Hall-probe mapping (Hengstberger et al. 2009; Perkins et al. 2001), with pick-up/search coils used only during the transient magnetization pulse itself (Eckert et al. 2001) ΓÇö never for the subsequent static state. This is the clearest domain-level confirmation of the mission's central concern: a coil channel is structurally blind to a persistent-mode trapped field because there is no dB/dt to sense once magnetization is complete, so a Hall+coil hybrid offers no incremental information in steady persistent-mode operation and only plausible value during the magnetization pulse (bandwidth/transient capture) or during in-machine AC ripple superimposed on the DC trapped field. The calibration-reference literature strongly favors NMR over any coil-based approach for the static state: the persistent-mode NMR magnet work (Yanagisawa et al. 2021, doi:10.1088/1361-6668/ac2120) shows a Hall sensor used only for coarse initial tracking, with the precision cross-check and long-term drift monitoring performed by an NMR Teslameter and a room-temperature solution-NMR probe ΓÇö exactly the material-diverse, independent reference the mission's decision framework calls for. Net assessment: this lane is a poor fit for the proposed Hall+coil hybrid's core value proposition (mutual drift calibration between two continuously co-observing channels), because the coil channel has no signal to contribute during the dominant (persistent/DC) operating mode; it is a plausible fit only as a transient/pulse-capture add-on during magnetization, where NMR (not the coil) remains the accepted absolute reference.

## Prose synthesis (domain: superconducting magnets / HTS field shaping / trapped-field rotors / superconducting motors-generators)

Field magnitudes in this lane are extreme relative to plasma-diagnostic work: bulk HTS trapped-field magnets now reach a documented record of 17.7 T (Patel et al. 2018, doi:10.1088/1361-6668/aad34c) with earlier 17.6 T (Durrell et al. 2014) and >17 T composite-stack (Huang et al. 2019/2020) results, all achieved by field-cooled or pulsed-field magnetization and then held as a static, persistent, essentially DC field for the operational lifetime of the magnet ΓÇö there is no continuous ramping once the magnet is charged. Superconducting-motor and generator field poles operate in the same DC-trapped regime at 35-77 K (Watasaki et al. 2021, doi:10.1088/1361-6668/abda5b; Climente-Alarcon et al. 2020, doi:10.1109/tasc.2020.2976603; Wang et al. 2023, doi:10.1088/1361-6668/acfcdf), with only the brief magnetization pulse itself (milliseconds, high dB/dt) constituting an AC/transient event. Cryostat access is the dominant spatial constraint: sensors are mounted at fixed points inside a cold bore or on a cryocooled rotor (4-77 K), commonly via linear or rotating Hall-sensor arrays (5-18 sensors) rather than a scanning bench probe, because in-situ access during operation is severely limited (Tsui et al. 2022, doi:10.1088/1361-6668/ac74e7). Temperature, not radiation, is the dominant environmental stressor, and cryogenic Hall behavior is quantitatively documented: InSb/GaAs epitaxial Hall sensors show sensitivity temperature coefficients that can be engineered down to ~0.001%/K in the 1.8-250 K range through doping (Oszwaldowski & Berus 2006, 2007), and other literature found during discovery (not yet independently ledger-verified here) reports sensitivity increasing by several percent from 320 K to 5 K before flattening below ~50 K ΓÇö i.e., cryogenic Hall sensors require their own low-temperature calibration curve, not a simple room-temperature transfer. The incumbent diagnostic for both trapped-field bulk magnets and superconducting-machine field poles is scanning or fixed-array Hall-probe mapping (Hengstberger et al. 2009; Perkins et al. 2001), with pick-up/search coils used only during the transient magnetization pulse itself (Eckert et al. 2001) ΓÇö never for the subsequent static state. This is the clearest domain-level confirmation of the mission's central concern: a coil channel is structurally blind to a persistent-mode trapped field because there is no dB/dt to sense once magnetization is complete, so a Hall+coil hybrid offers no incremental information in steady persistent-mode operation and only plausible value during the magnetization pulse (bandwidth/transient capture) or during in-machine AC ripple superimposed on the DC trapped field. The calibration-reference literature strongly favors NMR over any coil-based approach for the static state: the persistent-mode NMR magnet work (Yanagisawa et al. 2021, doi:10.1088/1361-6668/ac2120) shows a Hall sensor used only for coarse initial tracking, with the precision cross-check and long-term drift monitoring performed by an NMR Teslameter and a room-temperature solution-NMR probe ΓÇö exactly the material-diverse, independent reference the mission's decision framework calls for. Net assessment: this lane is a poor fit for the proposed Hall+coil hybrid's core value proposition (mutual drift calibration between two continuously co-observing channels), because the coil channel has no signal to contribute during the dominant (persistent/DC) operating mode; it is a plausible fit only as a transient/pulse-capture add-on during magnetization, where NMR (not the coil) remains the accepted absolute reference.

### Synthesis

Across the stellarator devices searched (W7-X, LHD, TJ-II, HSX-precedent facilities plus small university stellarators CNT, HIDRA, SCR-1), the dominant pre-plasma field-verification method is vacuum flux-surface mapping ΓÇö an electron gun injects a beam that is traced with a fluorescent screen, oscillating rod, or probe array, almost always at strongly reduced field (LHD mapped up to 2.75 T but commissioning-era work and the small devices operate at 10%-nominal or sub-0.1 T levels) and essentially DC/quasi-static; it is run as an infrequent commissioning campaign before (and occasionally after major maintenance to) plasma operation, not as a continuous diagnostic during shots. Its documented limitation, consistent across HIDRA, SCR-1, CNT, LHD, and TJ-II, is that the electron beam cannot survive in the presence of plasma, so it characterizes only the vacuum topology, which is then compared against a Biot-Savart/filament field model built from known (commanded or measured) coil currents ΓÇö this comparison is the de facto calibration reference, and it is realistically accessible only during scheduled commissioning windows, not on demand. ### Synthesis

Across the stellarator devices searched (W7-X, LHD, TJ-II, HSX-precedent facilities plus small university stellarators CNT, HIDRA, SCR-1), the dominant pre-plasma field-verification method is vacuum flux-surface mapping ΓÇö an electron gun injects a beam that is traced with a fluorescent screen, oscillating rod, or probe array, almost always at strongly reduced field (LHD mapped up to 2.75 T but commissioning-era work and the small devices operate at 10%-nominal or sub-0.1 T levels) and essentially DC/quasi-static; it is run as an infrequent commissioning campaign before (and occasionally after major maintenance to) plasma operation, not as a continuous diagnostic during shots. Its documented limitation, consistent across HIDRA, SCR-1, CNT, LHD, and TJ-II, is that the electron beam cannot survive in the presence of plasma, so it characterizes only the vacuum topology, which is then compared against a Biot-Savart/filament field model built from known (commanded or measured) coil currents ΓÇö this comparison is the de facto calibration reference, and it is realistically accessible only during scheduled commissioning windows, not on demand. Complementary to this, W7-X shows a documented three-stage workflow ΓÇö coil-accuracy design specification (LHD's 1993 analog gives ~1e-4 as the magnetic-accuracy criterion driven by winding, installation, cooldown, and electromagnetic-deformation errors unique to non-planar 3-D coils), post-construction error-field measurement (Lazerson 2018, building on the already-catalogued Otte 2016), and dedicated trim-coil correction hardware (Ki├ƒlinger & Andreeva 2005 design; F├╝llenbach et al. 2017 commissioning), with Lazerson reporting the measured error field required only ~5% of rated trim-coil current to correct. In-vessel installation constraints are evidenced concretely by TJ-II's 2022 helical Mirnov-array paper (routing coil arrays to match a non-axisymmetric heliac vessel) and by the small-device flux-mapping papers, which had to design detector geometry around tight, non-planar vacuum-vessel access. I found no literature ΓÇö despite targeted searches ΓÇö directly discussing a Hall+coil hybrid sensor for stellarator field mapping specifically; this appears to be a genuine gap rather than an oversight, and it should be labeled Unknown/unaddressed in the final synthesis rather than inferred favorably or unfavorably. Likewise, I found generic NMR-probe-calibrates-Hall-probe literature (accelerator/undulator magnet metrology) but no stellarator-specific application of NMR field mapping in-vessel; that absence should also be recorded as Unknown. None of the 10 new sources address radiation, temperature, or EMI survivability requirements for stellarator in-vessel sensors directly ΓÇö these commissioning-era and small-device papers predate or lack significant neutron fluence, so that criterion remains covered only by the pre-existing ITER/JET Hall-probe radiation literature already in the 06/10B lanes and should not be conflated with stellarator-specific evidence.

## Structured synthesis

**Fluxgate magnetometers.** Field range is typically sub-mT to a few mT with noise floors in the ~pT/ΓêÜHz to low-nT/ΓêÜHz range at 1 Hz depending on core design (Wei et al. 2021, S-new-2). Bandwidth is DC to a few kHz ΓÇö fluxgates are fundamentally a DC/low-frequency technology, complementary to inductive coils rather than competing with them on bandwidth. Greene et al. (2023) shows that even with good bulk-temperature compensation, thermal *gradients* across the sensor body (not just average temperature) directly corrupt baseline/offset stability ΓÇö a mechanism directly analogous to the Hall offset-drift problem this mission is investigating, and a caution that "temperature-compensated" claims must specify uniform vs. gradient conditions. Best-fit applications: geomagnetic observatories, spacecraft/space magnetometry, and (per the already-baselined ITER NBI fluxgate work) DC-field diagnostics in vacuum-compatible fusion auxiliary systems. Key limitation: no genuinely new *radiation-tolerance* source was found for fluxgate in this pass ΓÇö that remains a gap (the 06/10B baseline's ITER NBI fluxgate paper addresses radiation-hardness qualitatively but was not re-verified here since it's already in the ledger).

**AMR/GMR/TMR and planar Hall.** This family is the best-evidenced in this batch (4 new sources). AMR without integrated front-end electronics tolerates gamma doses to 200 krad(Si) at tens-of-nT resolution, while front-end electronics is the more radiation-vulnerable link (Sanz et al. 2012) ΓÇö directly parallel to the Hall+coil hybrid's own bias/readout-electronics vulnerability question. TMR sensors show no measurable degradation in sensitivity, noise, or transfer curve under 0ΓÇô5 Mrad(Si) ╬│/X-ray when kept biased during irradiation (2025, Science China) ΓÇö an order of magnitude beyond the AMR figure and worth flagging as a strong radiation-hard alternative/complement, though gamma/X-ray only (not neutron; per SOURCE_POLICY this must not be silently extrapolated to displacement damage). Bandwidth is DC-to-broadband (TMR review, An et al. 2025) ΓÇö genuinely single-channel DC+AC capability, which is a direct competitive challenge to the Hall+coil architecture's core value proposition and should be addressed explicitly in the comparison output. Planar Hall sensors (Lahav et al. 2024) achieve pT/ΓêÜHz noise but only in a sub-mT field range, illustrating a real sensitivity/range tradeoff. Best-fit applications: current sensing, power electronics, smart-grid metrology, and space magnetometry. Key limitation: none of the new sources here address in-vessel fusion deployment or neutron tolerance specifically ΓÇö that remains inferred by analogy to the semiconductor-radiation literature already in 06/10B, not observed.

**Fiber-optic / Faraday-effect current sensors.** Two new application-context sources were found, both tokamak-specific: the ITER FOCS work (Karabulut et al. 2019) shows the dominant *practical* limitation is not radiation but Faraday-mirror imperfection/detuning, correctable via a compensation formula if mirror detuning is independently measured ΓÇö an important "incumbent diagnostic limitation" data point distinct from the pure radiation-effects FOCS evidence already in 10B. The T-15MD concept paper (Sarancha et al. 2025) extends the application base to a third tokamak beyond the already-baselined ITER/EAST/JET instances. Field range/bandwidth: DC to tens of GHz, essentially unbounded by the sensor itself (limited by readout electronics), and immune to EMI ΓÇö the strongest single differentiator against both Hall and coil-only measurement. Best-fit application: total plasma current on long-pulse, high-radiation, or EMI-hostile machines (ITER, EAST). Key limitation: cost, fiber routing/mechanical stress sensitivity (birefringence from vibration/bending), and ΓÇö per 10B ΓÇö radiation-induced fiber attenuation/darkening, which is a genuine competing failure mode to the Hall+coil hybrid's own radiation risks.

**NMR magnetometry/probes.** Two new sources. Rodriguez et al. (2020) gives original evidence on the practical calibration-transfer limits of proton NMR ΓÇö sensitive-volume size and field-inhomogeneity set the achievable transfer accuracy, directly relevant to the DECISION_FRAMEWORK's requirement for a "traceable magnet/NMR/fluxgate" bench reference. Bl├╝mler et al. (2025, published in the mission's own target comparator journal, Review of Scientific Instruments) demonstrates cryogenic gaseous 3He NMR reaching ~10Γü╗┬╣┬▓ relative precision ΓÇö the practical ceiling for NMR-class absolute references, but only under cryogenic, quasi-static conditions. Bandwidth: essentially DC/quasi-static only in both sources; NMR cannot itself track transient plasma fields. Best-fit application: absolute bench/lab calibration reference for the Hall+coil hybrid, not an in-situ HSX sensor. Key limitation: needs a homogeneous field region and (for high precision) cryogenic operation ΓÇö neither is available in-vessel.

**SQUID magnetometers.** Two new sources, one foundational review (Fagaly 2006) and one historical application paper (Goree & Fuller 1976, paleomagnetism). Sensitivity is fT/ΓêÜHz to sub-fT/ΓêÜHz class ΓÇö orders of magnitude beyond any solid-state alternative in this ledger ΓÇö but requires cryogenic cooling (~4ΓÇô9 K for low-Tc, ~77 K for high-Tc) and has a narrow linear dynamic range (sub-nT without feedback linearization, per search-derived context on Josephson-junction flux penetration limits ΓÇö this specific quantitative claim was not independently verified against a citable peer-reviewed source in this pass and should be treated as **inferred/unverified** context rather than a ledger-backed claim). Typical uses: biomagnetism (MEG/MCG), geophysics/paleomagnetism, materials characterization. No new peer-reviewed source was found that directly and quantitatively documents SQUID *unsuitability* for high-field, radiation, or elevated-temperature fusion environments ΓÇö the mission's own reasoning (cryogenic incompatibility with in-vessel heat loads, superconductor radiation damage, narrow field/dynamic range) is a defensible **inference** from the general SQUID operating-envelope evidence here plus the (already-baselined) HTS radiation-damage literature, not a directly observed claim about SQUID sensors specifically in a fusion device. This is a genuine gap worth flagging rather than papering over.

**NV-center / quantum magnetometry.** Two new foundational reviews (Rondin et al. 2014; Doherty et al. 2013) cover NV-center physics, sensitivity regimes (down to fT/ΓêÜHz-class in favorable ensemble configurations, though single-NV sensitivity is far weaker), and general temperature dependence. Neither addresses radiation tolerance or fusion/plasma applicability directly ΓÇö both predate that application discussion. A 2026 preprint, "High Field Diamond Magnetometry Towards Tokamak Diagnostics" (Graham, Stephen, Newman, Edmonds, Markham, Morley; arXiv 2601.13413), directly targets tokamak-relevant NV magnetometry at ΓëÑ1 T and explicitly raises NV radiation-hardness as a motivation ΓÇö but **this is currently only an arXiv preprint with no verified peer-reviewed publication**, so per SOURCE_POLICY it is excluded from the verified ledger above and is recorded here only as a discovery lead for future re-checking, not as evidence. **This is the weakest-evidenced family in this batch**: TRL for fusion-relevant NV magnetometry is low, and no peer-reviewed radiation-tolerance or high-field-tokamak-deployment data currently exists ΓÇö an honest, load-bearing gap rather than a forced citation.

**Standalone (non-hybrid) Hall/inductive baseline.** Given that folder 06 already carries extensive standalone Hall-probe, Mirnov-coil, Rogowski-coil, and B-dot literature (per `baseline_06_application_rows.txt`, e.g., S0068ΓÇôS0117, S0225), this family did not need heavy new sourcing. Two new sources were added for cross-checking and diversification: Ripka & Janosek (2010) is a widely cited, single-paper cross-technology review (Hall, fluxgate, AMR/GMR/TMR) useful as an anchor for sanity-checking the family-specific figures above against one internally consistent source; Arpaia et al. (2019) documents a standalone rotating-coil (inductive) magnetometer used for spatial field-harmonic mapping on HL-LHC superconducting accelerator-magnet triplets ΓÇö a concrete, non-fusion, high-field application context that is directly relevant to the mission's "accelerator magnets... when technically transferable" application lane, and to the DC-field-mapping capability gap of static (non-rotating) coil sensing.

## Coverage against the acceptance gate

All 7 requested technology families have at least one genuinely new, verified peer-reviewed source; 6 of 7 have 2+ (fluxgate, AMR/GMR/TMR/planar Hall, fiber-optic, NMR, NV-center, standalone baseline), and SQUID has 1 strong review plus 1 narrower historical application paper. Total: 16 new sources, all confirmed absent from the 357-DOI dedup baseline. Two explicit, stated gaps: (1) no peer-reviewed source on SQUID unsuitability specifically in fusion/radiation environments ΓÇö the reasoning is inferred from general operating-envelope evidence plus baselined HTS radiation literature; (2) no peer-reviewed source (only a 2026 preprint) on NV-center radiation tolerance or high-field tokamak deployment.

## Structured synthesis

**Fluxgate magnetometers.** Field range is typically sub-mT to a few mT with noise floors in the ~pT/ΓêÜHz to low-nT/ΓêÜHz range at 1 Hz depending on core design (Wei et al. 2021, S-new-2). Bandwidth is DC to a few kHz ΓÇö fluxgates are fundamentally a DC/low-frequency technology, complementary to inductive coils rather than competing with them on bandwidth. Greene et al. (2023) shows that even with good bulk-temperature compensation, thermal *gradients* across the sensor body (not just average temperature) directly corrupt baseline/offset stability ΓÇö a mechanism directly analogous to the Hall offset-drift problem this mission is investigating, and a caution that "temperature-compensated" claims must specify uniform vs. gradient conditions. Best-fit applications: geomagnetic observatories, spacecraft/space magnetometry, and (per the already-baselined ITER NBI fluxgate work) DC-field diagnostics in vacuum-compatible fusion auxiliary systems. Key limitation: no genuinely new *radiation-tolerance* source was found for fluxgate in this pass ΓÇö that remains a gap (the 06/10B baseline's ITER NBI fluxgate paper addresses radiation-hardness qualitatively but was not re-verified here since it's already in the ledger).

**AMR/GMR/TMR and planar Hall.** This family is the best-evidenced in this batch (4 new sources). AMR without integrated front-end electronics tolerates gamma doses to 200 krad(Si) at tens-of-nT resolution, while front-end electronics is the more radiation-vulnerable link (Sanz et al. 2012) ΓÇö directly parallel to the Hall+coil hybrid's own bias/readout-electronics vulnerability question. TMR sensors show no measurable degradation in sensitivity, noise, or transfer curve under 0ΓÇô5 Mrad(Si) ╬│/X-ray when kept biased during irradiation (2025, Science China) ΓÇö an order of magnitude beyond the AMR figure and worth flagging as a strong radiation-hard alternative/complement, though gamma/X-ray only (not neutron; per SOURCE_POLICY this must not be silently extrapolated to displacement damage). Bandwidth is DC-to-broadband (TMR review, An et al. 2025) ΓÇö genuinely single-channel DC+AC capability, which is a direct competitive challenge to the Hall+coil architecture's core value proposition and should be addressed explicitly in the comparison output. Planar Hall sensors (Lahav et al. 2024) achieve pT/ΓêÜHz noise but only in a sub-mT field range, illustrating a real sensitivity/range tradeoff. Best-fit applications: current sensing, power electronics, smart-grid metrology, and space magnetometry. Key limitation: none of the new sources here address in-vessel fusion deployment or neutron tolerance specifically ΓÇö that remains inferred by analogy to the semiconductor-radiation literature already in 06/10B, not observed.

**Fiber-optic / Faraday-effect current sensors.** Two new application-context sources were found, both tokamak-specific: the ITER FOCS work (Karabulut et al. 2019) shows the dominant *practical* limitation is not radiation but Faraday-mirror imperfection/detuning, correctable via a compensation formula if mirror detuning is independently measured ΓÇö an important "incumbent diagnostic limitation" data point distinct from the pure radiation-effects FOCS evidence already in 10B. The T-15MD concept paper (Sarancha et al. 2025) extends the application base to a third tokamak beyond the already-baselined ITER/EAST/JET instances. Field range/bandwidth: DC to tens of GHz, essentially unbounded by the sensor itself (limited by readout electronics), and immune to EMI ΓÇö the strongest single differentiator against both Hall and coil-only measurement. Best-fit application: total plasma current on long-pulse, high-radiation, or EMI-hostile machines (ITER, EAST). Key limitation: cost, fiber routing/mechanical stress sensitivity (birefringence from vibration/bending), and ΓÇö per 10B ΓÇö radiation-induced fiber attenuation/darkening, which is a genuine competing failure mode to the Hall+coil hybrid's own radiation risks.

**NMR magnetometry/probes.** Two new sources. Rodriguez et al. (2020) gives original evidence on the practical calibration-transfer limits of proton NMR ΓÇö sensitive-volume size and field-inhomogeneity set the achievable transfer accuracy, directly relevant to the DECISION_FRAMEWORK's requirement for a "traceable magnet/NMR/fluxgate" bench reference. Bl├╝mler et al. (2025, published in the mission's own target comparator journal, Review of Scientific Instruments) demonstrates cryogenic gaseous 3He NMR reaching ~10Γü╗┬╣┬▓ relative precision ΓÇö the practical ceiling for NMR-class absolute references, but only under cryogenic, quasi-static conditions. Bandwidth: essentially DC/quasi-static only in both sources; NMR cannot itself track transient plasma fields. Best-fit application: absolute bench/lab calibration reference for the Hall+coil hybrid, not an in-situ HSX sensor. Key limitation: needs a homogeneous field region and (for high precision) cryogenic operation ΓÇö neither is available in-vessel.

**SQUID magnetometers.** Two new sources, one foundational review (Fagaly 2006) and one historical application paper (Goree & Fuller 1976, paleomagnetism). Sensitivity is fT/ΓêÜHz to sub-fT/ΓêÜHz class ΓÇö orders of magnitude beyond any solid-state alternative in this ledger ΓÇö but requires cryogenic cooling (~4ΓÇô9 K for low-Tc, ~77 K for high-Tc) and has a narrow linear dynamic range (sub-nT without feedback linearization, per search-derived context on Josephson-junction flux penetration limits ΓÇö this specific quantitative claim was not independently verified against a citable peer-reviewed source in this pass and should be treated as **inferred/unverified** context rather than a ledger-backed claim). Typical uses: biomagnetism (MEG/MCG), geophysics/paleomagnetism, materials characterization. No new peer-reviewed source was found that directly and quantitatively documents SQUID *unsuitability* for high-field, radiation, or elevated-temperature fusion environments ΓÇö the mission's own reasoning (cryogenic incompatibility with in-vessel heat loads, superconductor radiation damage, narrow field/dynamic range) is a defensible **inference** from the general SQUID operating-envelope evidence here plus the (already-baselined) HTS radiation-damage literature, not a directly observed claim about SQUID sensors specifically in a fusion device. This is a genuine gap worth flagging rather than papering over.

**NV-center / quantum magnetometry.** Two new foundational reviews (Rondin et al. 2014; Doherty et al. 2013) cover NV-center physics, sensitivity regimes (down to fT/ΓêÜHz-class in favorable ensemble configurations, though single-NV sensitivity is far weaker), and general temperature dependence. Neither addresses radiation tolerance or fusion/plasma applicability directly ΓÇö both predate that application discussion. A 2026 preprint, "High Field Diamond Magnetometry Towards Tokamak Diagnostics" (Graham, Stephen, Newman, Edmonds, Markham, Morley; arXiv 2601.13413), directly targets tokamak-relevant NV magnetometry at ΓëÑ1 T and explicitly raises NV radiation-hardness as a motivation ΓÇö but **this is currently only an arXiv preprint with no verified peer-reviewed publication**, so per SOURCE_POLICY it is excluded from the verified ledger above and is recorded here only as a discovery lead for future re-checking, not as evidence. **This is the weakest-evidenced family in this batch**: TRL for fusion-relevant NV magnetometry is low, and no peer-reviewed radiation-tolerance or high-field-tokamak-deployment data currently exists ΓÇö an honest, load-bearing gap rather than a forced citation.

**Standalone (non-hybrid) Hall/inductive baseline.** Given that folder 06 already carries extensive standalone Hall-probe, Mirnov-coil, Rogowski-coil, and B-dot literature (per `baseline_06_application_rows.txt`, e.g., S0068ΓÇôS0117, S0225), this family did not need heavy new sourcing. Two new sources were added for cross-checking and diversification: Ripka & Janosek (2010) is a widely cited, single-paper cross-technology review (Hall, fluxgate, AMR/GMR/TMR) useful as an anchor for sanity-checking the family-specific figures above against one internally consistent source; Arpaia et al. (2019) documents a standalone rotating-coil (inductive) magnetometer used for spatial field-harmonic mapping on HL-LHC superconducting accelerator-magnet triplets ΓÇö a concrete, non-fusion, high-field application context that is directly relevant to the mission's "accelerator magnets... when technically transferable" application lane, and to the DC-field-mapping capability gap of static (non-rotating) coil sensing.

## Coverage against the acceptance gate

All 7 requested technology families have at least one genuinely new, verified peer-reviewed source; 6 of 7 have 2+ (fluxgate, AMR/GMR/TMR/planar Hall, fiber-optic, NMR, NV-center, standalone baseline), and SQUID has 1 strong review plus 1 narrower historical application paper. Total: 16 new sources, all confirmed absent from the 357-DOI dedup baseline. Two explicit, stated gaps: (1) no peer-reviewed source on SQUID unsuitability specifically in fusion/radiation environments ΓÇö the reasoning is inferred from general operating-envelope evidence plus baselined HTS radiation literature; (2) no peer-reviewed source (only a 2026 preprint) on NV-center radiation tolerance or high-field tokamak deployment.

## Structured synthesis

**Fluxgate magnetometers.** Field range is typically sub-mT to a few mT with noise floors in the ~pT/ΓêÜHz to low-nT/ΓêÜHz range at 1 Hz depending on core design (Wei et al. 2021, S-new-2). Bandwidth is DC to a few kHz ΓÇö fluxgates are fundamentally a DC/low-frequency technology, complementary to inductive coils rather than competing with them on bandwidth. Greene et al. (2023) shows that even with good bulk-temperature compensation, thermal *gradients* across the sensor body (not just average temperature) directly corrupt baseline/offset stability ΓÇö a mechanism directly analogous to the Hall offset-drift problem this mission is investigating, and a caution that "temperature-compensated" claims must specify uniform vs. gradient conditions. Best-fit applications: geomagnetic observatories, spacecraft/space magnetometry, and (per the already-baselined ITER NBI fluxgate work) DC-field diagnostics in vacuum-compatible fusion auxiliary systems. Key limitation: no genuinely new *radiation-tolerance* source was found for fluxgate in this pass ΓÇö that remains a gap (the 06/10B baseline's ITER NBI fluxgate paper addresses radiation-hardness qualitatively but was not re-verified here since it's already in the ledger).

**AMR/GMR/TMR and planar Hall.** This family is the best-evidenced in this batch (4 new sources). AMR without integrated front-end electronics tolerates gamma doses to 200 krad(Si) at tens-of-nT resolution, while front-end electronics is the more radiation-vulnerable link (Sanz et al. 2012) ΓÇö directly parallel to the Hall+coil hybrid's own bias/readout-electronics vulnerability question. TMR sensors show no measurable degradation in sensitivity, noise, or transfer curve under 0ΓÇô5 Mrad(Si) ╬│/X-ray when kept biased during irradiation (2025, Science China) ΓÇö an order of magnitude beyond the AMR figure and worth flagging as a strong radiation-hard alternative/complement, though gamma/X-ray only (not neutron; per SOURCE_POLICY this must not be silently extrapolated to displacement damage). Bandwidth is DC-to-broadband (TMR review, An et al. 2025) ΓÇö genuinely single-channel DC+AC capability, which is a direct competitive challenge to the Hall+coil architecture's core value proposition and should be addressed explicitly in the comparison output. Planar Hall sensors (Lahav et al. 2024) achieve pT/ΓêÜHz noise but only in a sub-mT field range, illustrating a real sensitivity/range tradeoff. Best-fit applications: current sensing, power electronics, smart-grid metrology, and space magnetometry. Key limitation: none of the new sources here address in-vessel fusion deployment or neutron tolerance specifically ΓÇö that remains inferred by analogy to the semiconductor-radiation literature already in 06/10B, not observed.

**Fiber-optic / Faraday-effect current sensors.** Two new application-context sources were found, both tokamak-specific: the ITER FOCS work (Karabulut et al. 2019) shows the dominant *practical* limitation is not radiation but Faraday-mirror imperfection/detuning, correctable via a compensation formula if mirror detuning is independently measured ΓÇö an important "incumbent diagnostic limitation" data point distinct from the pure radiation-effects FOCS evidence already in 10B. The T-15MD concept paper (Sarancha et al. 2025) extends the application base to a third tokamak beyond the already-baselined ITER/EAST/JET instances. Field range/bandwidth: DC to tens of GHz, essentially unbounded by the sensor itself (limited by readout electronics), and immune to EMI ΓÇö the strongest single differentiator against both Hall and coil-only measurement. Best-fit application: total plasma current on long-pulse, high-radiation, or EMI-hostile machines (ITER, EAST). Key limitation: cost, fiber routing/mechanical stress sensitivity (birefringence from vibration/bending), and ΓÇö per 10B ΓÇö radiation-induced fiber attenuation/darkening, which is a genuine competing failure mode to the Hall+coil hybrid's own radiation risks.

**NMR magnetometry/probes.** Two new sources. Rodriguez et al. (2020) gives original evidence on the practical calibration-transfer limits of proton NMR ΓÇö sensitive-volume size and field-inhomogeneity set the achievable transfer accuracy, directly relevant to the DECISION_FRAMEWORK's requirement for a "traceable magnet/NMR/fluxgate" bench reference. Bl├╝mler et al. (2025, published in the mission's own target comparator journal, Review of Scientific Instruments) demonstrates cryogenic gaseous 3He NMR reaching ~10Γü╗┬╣┬▓ relative precision ΓÇö the practical ceiling for NMR-class absolute references, but only under cryogenic, quasi-static conditions. Bandwidth: essentially DC/quasi-static only in both sources; NMR cannot itself track transient plasma fields. Best-fit application: absolute bench/lab calibration reference for the Hall+coil hybrid, not an in-situ HSX sensor. Key limitation: needs a homogeneous field region and (for high precision) cryogenic operation ΓÇö neither is available in-vessel.

**SQUID magnetometers.** Two new sources, one foundational review (Fagaly 2006) and one historical application paper (Goree & Fuller 1976, paleomagnetism). Sensitivity is fT/ΓêÜHz to sub-fT/ΓêÜHz class ΓÇö orders of magnitude beyond any solid-state alternative in this ledger ΓÇö but requires cryogenic cooling (~4ΓÇô9 K for low-Tc, ~77 K for high-Tc) and has a narrow linear dynamic range (sub-nT without feedback linearization, per search-derived context on Josephson-junction flux penetration limits ΓÇö this specific quantitative claim was not independently verified against a citable peer-reviewed source in this pass and should be treated as **inferred/unverified** context rather than a ledger-backed claim). Typical uses: biomagnetism (MEG/MCG), geophysics/paleomagnetism, materials characterization. No new peer-reviewed source was found that directly and quantitatively documents SQUID *unsuitability* for high-field, radiation, or elevated-temperature fusion environments ΓÇö the mission's own reasoning (cryogenic incompatibility with in-vessel heat loads, superconductor radiation damage, narrow field/dynamic range) is a defensible **inference** from the general SQUID operating-envelope evidence here plus the (already-baselined) HTS radiation-damage literature, not a directly observed claim about SQUID sensors specifically in a fusion device. This is a genuine gap worth flagging rather than papering over.

**NV-center / quantum magnetometry.** Two new foundational reviews (Rondin et al. 2014; Doherty et al. 2013) cover NV-center physics, sensitivity regimes (down to fT/ΓêÜHz-class in favorable ensemble configurations, though single-NV sensitivity is far weaker), and general temperature dependence. Neither addresses radiation tolerance or fusion/plasma applicability directly ΓÇö both predate that application discussion. A 2026 preprint, "High Field Diamond Magnetometry Towards Tokamak Diagnostics" (Graham, Stephen, Newman, Edmonds, Markham, Morley; arXiv 2601.13413), directly targets tokamak-relevant NV magnetometry at ΓëÑ1 T and explicitly raises NV radiation-hardness as a motivation ΓÇö but **this is currently only an arXiv preprint with no verified peer-reviewed publication**, so per SOURCE_POLICY it is excluded from the verified ledger above and is recorded here only as a discovery lead for future re-checking, not as evidence. **This is the weakest-evidenced family in this batch**: TRL for fusion-relevant NV magnetometry is low, and no peer-reviewed radiation-tolerance or high-field-tokamak-deployment data currently exists ΓÇö an honest, load-bearing gap rather than a forced citation.

**Standalone (non-hybrid) Hall/inductive baseline.** Given that folder 06 already carries extensive standalone Hall-probe, Mirnov-coil, Rogowski-coil, and B-dot literature (per `baseline_06_application_rows.txt`, e.g., S0068ΓÇôS0117, S0225), this family did not need heavy new sourcing. Two new sources were added for cross-checking and diversification: Ripka & Janosek (2010) is a widely cited, single-paper cross-technology review (Hall, fluxgate, AMR/GMR/TMR) useful as an anchor for sanity-checking the family-specific figures above against one internally consistent source; Arpaia et al. (2019) documents a standalone rotating-coil (inductive) magnetometer used for spatial field-harmonic mapping on HL-LHC superconducting accelerator-magnet triplets ΓÇö a concrete, non-fusion, high-field application context that is directly relevant to the mission's "accelerator magnets... when technically transferable" application lane, and to the DC-field-mapping capability gap of static (non-rotating) coil sensing.

## Coverage against the acceptance gate

All 7 requested technology families have at least one genuinely new, verified peer-reviewed source; 6 of 7 have 2+ (fluxgate, AMR/GMR/TMR/planar Hall, fiber-optic, NMR, NV-center, standalone baseline), and SQUID has 1 strong review plus 1 narrower historical application paper. Total: 16 new sources, all confirmed absent from the 357-DOI dedup baseline. Two explicit, stated gaps: (1) no peer-reviewed source on SQUID unsuitability specifically in fusion/radiation environments ΓÇö the reasoning is inferred from general operating-envelope evidence plus baselined HTS radiation literature; (2) no peer-reviewed source (only a 2026 preprint) on NV-center radiation tolerance or high-field tokamak deployment.

### Synthesis (prose)

The current group landscape splits cleanly by application maturity. Long-pulse tokamak/stellarator magnetic diagnostics has the deepest, most identifiable bench of active groups ΓÇö KFE/KSTAR (Korea), ITER Organization plus its ITPA Diagnostics Topical Group, IPP Greifswald/W7-X, and especially the JET RHP lineage (Consorzio CREATE/RFX, Lviv Polytechnic, and IPP CAS Prague) ΓÇö all traceable to named authors, institutional affiliations, and directly on-topic peer-reviewed papers from 2022ΓÇô2026, several published in the same journal (Nuclear Fusion, Plasma Physics and Controlled Fusion) that seeded this mission. Radiation-hard Hall sensing specifically is concentrated in a tight, collaborating EU network (Lviv Polytechnic material/device work feeding into JET installations run by Consorzio CREATE/RFX, with IPP CAS Prague now leading the ITER/DEMO antimony-Hall successor work) rather than being spread across many independent labs ΓÇö this is a small, mature, and well-documented community, not a thin one. Pulsed-power/z-pinch (Sandia Z/Mykonos) and accelerator/HTS field-mapping (CERN EP-DT, Cambridge Bulk Superconductivity Group) are thinner in fusion-specific relevance: official pages confirm active, currently operating magnetic-diagnostics or field-mapping programs, but the best available supporting publications are either broad program overviews (Sandia) or genuinely different-domain metrology (CERN accelerator, Cambridge HTS) rather than papers specifically about Hall+coil hybrid sensing under radiation. Geographically, the landscape is bimodal: a Europe/Asia fusion-diagnostics cluster (Czech Republic, Italy/Ukraine, Germany, Korea) doing the most directly relevant work, versus US national-lab and CERN facilities doing adjacent, technically transferable but application-distinct magnetic metrology. One structural caveat worth flagging: several "groups" here are not single labs with one homepage but multi-institution author collaborations (the JET RHP work spans three institutions), so official-page verification is necessarily weaker for those than for single-institution labs like KFE, IPP CAS, or Cambridge.
